p.text: She plays tennis every Saturday.
p.correction: She plays tennis every Saturday.
p.explanation: With he, she or it in the present simple, the verb ends in -s: she plays.

p.text: My brother watch TV after dinner.
p.correction: My brother watches TV after dinner.
p.explanation: My brother is one person (he), so the verb needs -es: watches.

p.text: There are two cats in the garden.
p.correction: There are two cats in the garden.
p.explanation: We use there are with a plural noun (two cats).

p.text: There is five books on the desk.
p.correction: There are five books on the desk.
p.explanation: Five books is plural, so we say there are, not there is.

p.text: My sister _____ in a bank.
p.correction: My sister works in a bank.
p.explanation: My sister is she, so the present simple verb needs -s: works. 'Work' has no -s, and 'working' and 'are working' do not fit.

p.text: _____ your parents at home now?
p.correction: Are your parents at home now?
p.explanation: Parents is plural, so we use are. Is is for one person, and do/does are not used with be.

p.text: Tom _____ two brothers and a sister.
p.correction: Tom has two brothers and a sister.
p.explanation: Tom is he, so we use has (not have) to talk about what he has.

p.text: There _____ a big park near my house, so we play there every Sunday.
p.correction: There is a big park near my house, so we play there every Sunday.
p.explanation: A big park is one thing, so we use there is.

p.text: Our neighbour is a very good _____ and she sings every day.
p.correction: Our neighbour is a very good singer and she sings every day.
p.explanation: A person who sings is a singer; we need a noun after 'a very good'.

p.text: Everyone in my class likes the new teacher.
p.correction: Everyone in my class likes the new teacher.
p.explanation: Everyone is singular, so the verb takes -s: likes.

p.text: Everybody are ready for the school trip.
p.correction: Everybody is ready for the school trip.
p.explanation: Everybody means all people but is grammatically singular, so we use is.

p.text: Does your brother play the guitar?
p.correction: Does your brother play the guitar?
p.explanation: In questions with he, she or it we use does, and the main verb has no -s.

p.text: Does your sister likes pizza with pineapple?
p.correction: Does your sister like pizza with pineapple?
p.explanation: After does, the main verb is in its base form: like, not likes.

p.text: Nobody _____ the answer to the last question.
p.correction: Nobody knows the answer to the last question.
p.explanation: Nobody is singular, so the present simple verb takes -s: knows. 'Know' is plural, and the other options are not correct forms.

p.text: _____ Maria go to school by bus?
p.correction: Does Maria go to school by bus?
p.explanation: Maria is she, so a present simple question uses does. 'Do' is for I/you/we/they, and is/are cannot go before the verb 'go'.

p.text: Listen! Everyone in the room _____ laughing at the joke.
p.correction: Listen! Everyone in the room is laughing at the joke.
p.explanation: Everyone is singular, and 'Listen!' shows the action is happening now, so we need is laughing.

p.text: _____ your mum work on Saturdays these days?
p.correction: Does your mum work on Saturdays these days?
p.explanation: Your mum is she, so a present simple question starts with does.

p.text: My room _____ two beds.
p.correction: My room has got two beds.
p.explanation: My room is singular, so we use has got (not have got) to say what it contains.
p.leadInSentence: There are two beds in my room.

p.text: Each of the rooms has a view of the sea.
p.correction: Each of the rooms has a view of the sea.
p.explanation: Each is singular, even before 'of the rooms', so the verb is has.

p.text: The news about the new stadium are very exciting.
p.correction: The news about the new stadium is very exciting.
p.explanation: News looks plural but is uncountable and singular, so it takes is.

p.text: Mathematics has always been my favourite subject at school.
p.correction: Mathematics has always been my favourite subject at school.
p.explanation: Mathematics ends in -s but is singular, so it takes has.

p.text: Every child in the village have a bicycle.
p.correction: Every child in the village has a bicycle.
p.explanation: Every is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb, so we say has.
p.grammarPhrase: Every child in the village has
p.mistakeType: plural verb after every + singular noun

p.text: The police _____ looking for a missing child.
p.correction: The police are looking for a missing child.
p.explanation: Police is always plural, so we use are. Is and has do not agree with it, and does cannot combine with looking.

p.text: Ten kilometres _____ a long way to walk in one day.
p.correction: Ten kilometres is a long way to walk in one day.
p.explanation: A distance is treated as one amount, so we use the singular is. Are and were are plural, and have cannot make this sentence.
p.grammarPhrase: Ten kilometres is a long way

p.text: Either Sam or his parents _____ going to collect you tonight.
p.correction: Either Sam or his parents are going to collect you tonight.
p.explanation: With either...or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'His parents' is plural, so we use are.

p.text: _____ drives.
p.correction: Neither of my parents drives.
p.explanation: Neither of is followed by a singular verb in careful English, so we say drives.
p.leadInSentence: My mother doesn't drive, and my father doesn't drive either.

p.text: The _____ that the match was cancelled disappointed everyone.
p.correction: The announcement that the match was cancelled disappointed everyone.
p.explanation: After 'the' we need a noun. The noun from announce is announcement.

p.text: A number of students have asked for extra practice before the exam.
p.correction: A number of students have asked for extra practice before the exam.
p.explanation: A number of means 'several' and takes a plural verb: have asked.

p.text: The number of students taking the course have risen sharply this year.
p.correction: The number of students taking the course has risen sharply this year.
p.explanation: The number of is about the figure itself, which is singular, so we use has.
p.grammarPhrase: The number of students taking the course has
p.mistakeType: plural verb after the number of

p.text: The teacher, along with her students, is visiting the science museum on Friday.
p.correction: The teacher, along with her students, is visiting the science museum on Friday.
p.explanation: Along with does not make the subject plural, so the verb agrees with the teacher: is.
p.grammarPhrase: The teacher, along with her students, is

p.text: Neither the manager nor the employees was told about the changes.
p.correction: Neither the manager nor the employees were told about the changes.
p.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'The employees' is plural, so we need were.
p.mistakeType: verb agrees with wrong subject after neither...nor

p.text: Physics _____ one of the hardest subjects I have ever studied.
p.correction: Physics is one of the hardest subjects I have ever studied.
p.explanation: Physics ends in -s but is a single subject, so it takes the singular is. The other options are plural or use the wrong form.
p.grammarPhrase: Physics is one of the hardest

p.text: What worries me most _____ the lack of clear instructions.
p.correction: What worries me most is the lack of clear instructions.
p.explanation: A what-clause is followed by a singular verb when the thing it points to is singular: the lack of clear instructions.

p.text: Fifty pounds _____ a lot of money for a T-shirt, isn't it?
p.correction: Fifty pounds is a lot of money for a T-shirt, isn't it?
p.explanation: An amount of money is thought of as one sum, so it takes a singular verb. The tag isn't it confirms is.

p.text: _____ is a long holiday.
p.correction: What I really need is a long holiday.
p.explanation: A what-clause can introduce the thing we want to stress, followed by the singular verb is.
p.leadInSentence: I really need a long holiday.

p.text: The majority of voters were opposed to the _____ of a new parking tax.
p.correction: The majority of voters were opposed to the introduction of a new parking tax.
p.explanation: After 'the' and before 'of', we need a noun. The noun from introduce is introduction.

p.text: The majority of the villagers were opposed to the new bypass.
p.correction: The majority of the villagers were opposed to the new bypass.
p.explanation: The majority of followed by a plural noun takes a plural verb: were.
p.grammarPhrase: The majority of the villagers were

p.text: A great number of complaints has been received since the policy was announced.
p.correction: A great number of complaints have been received since the policy was announced.
p.explanation: A great number of means 'many', so the verb is plural: have been received.
p.mistakeType: singular verb after a number of

p.text: Either the contractors or the architect is going to have to explain the delay.
p.correction: Either the contractors or the architect is going to have to explain the delay.
p.explanation: With either...or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'The architect' is singular, so we use is.

p.text: The extent of the damage, as well as the long-term costs, _____ still being assessed.
p.correction: The extent of the damage, as well as the long-term costs, is still being assessed.
p.explanation: The subject is 'the extent' (singular); 'as well as' adds information without making it plural. Are, were and have been are plural forms.

p.text: Everyone who attended the workshop, regardless of their background, _____ encouraged to contribute.
p.correction: Everyone who attended the workshop, regardless of their background, was encouraged to contribute.
p.explanation: Everyone is singular, even though 'their' follows. Of the options, only was is singular and fits the past event; the rest are plural.

p.text: The number of applicants _____ doubled since the scholarship was announced.
p.correction: The number of applicants has doubled since the scholarship was announced.
p.explanation: The number of takes a singular verb, and since... needs the present perfect: has doubled.

p.text: Economics _____ widely regarded as the most influential social science today.
p.correction: Economics is widely regarded as the most influential social science today.
p.explanation: Economics is a single subject, so it takes a singular verb. 'Today' shows present tense.

p.text: The _____ the residents have objected to the plan.
p.correction: The majority of the residents have objected to the plan.
p.explanation: The majority of plus a plural noun means 'most', and the verb stays plural: have objected.
p.grammarPhrase: The majority of the residents have
p.leadInSentence: Most of the residents have objected to the plan.

p.text: Nobody in the department has ever questioned her professional _____.
p.correction: Nobody in the department has ever questioned her professional honesty.
p.explanation: After a possessive and adjective we need a noun. The noun from honest is honesty.

p.text: What matters most to the organisers is the safety of all the participants.
p.correction: What matters most to the organisers is the safety of all the participants.
p.explanation: In a what-cleft with a singular complement (the safety), the verb is singular: is.
p.grammarPhrase: What matters most to the organisers is

p.text: The majority of the evidence presented at the hearing were circumstantial.
p.correction: The majority of the evidence presented at the hearing was circumstantial.
p.explanation: Evidence is uncountable, so 'the majority of the evidence' takes a singular verb: was.

p.text: The remains of the medieval abbey, which _____ discovered beneath a car park, are now open to visitors.
p.correction: The remains of the medieval abbey, which were discovered beneath a car park, are now open to visitors.
p.explanation: The relative pronoun which refers to 'the remains', a plural noun, so the verb is plural: were. Was, has been and is are singular.

p.text: A large proportion of the budget _____ been spent on administration, which is deeply troubling.
p.correction: A large proportion of the budget has been spent on administration, which is deeply troubling.
p.explanation: The budget is singular, so 'a large proportion of the budget' takes a singular verb: has been spent. Have, are and were are plural.

p.text: Neither the ministers nor the prime minister herself _____ been willing to accept responsibility, so far.
p.correction: Neither the ministers nor the prime minister herself has been willing to accept responsibility, so far.
p.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'The prime minister' is singular, so we need has.

p.text: The _____ festival is falling every year.
p.correction: The number of visitors to the festival is falling every year.
p.explanation: The number of takes a singular verb, so we say is falling.
p.leadInSentence: The festival attracts fewer visitors every year.

p.text: The police _____ arrested the culprit.
p.correction: The police are rumoured to have arrested the culprit.
p.explanation: Police is always plural, so the passive verb is are rumoured.
p.leadInSentence: It is rumoured that the police have arrested the culprit.

p.text: The sheer _____ of the regulations, together with their frequent revision, makes compliance a challenge.
p.correction: The sheer complexity of the regulations, together with their frequent revision, makes compliance a challenge.
p.explanation: After 'sheer' and before 'of', we need a noun. The noun from complex is complexity; the singular subject takes makes.

p.text: My cat is more small than your dog.
p.correction: My cat is smaller than your dog.
p.explanation: Small is a short adjective, so we add -er: smaller. We do not use more with short adjectives.

p.text: Maths is the most easy subject for me.
p.correction: Maths is the easiest subject for me.
p.explanation: Easy is a short adjective, so the superlative is easiest (y changes to i). We do not say most easy.

p.text: Summer is hotter than spring in my country.
p.correction: Summer is hotter than spring in my country.
p.explanation: Hot doubles the t and adds -er: hotter. We use than to compare two things.

p.text: Ben is _____ than his sister.
p.correction: Ben is older than his sister.
p.explanation: Old is a short adjective, so the comparative is older. Oldest is a superlative, and more old is not used with short adjectives.

p.text: This is the _____ pizza in town.
p.correction: This is the best pizza in town.
p.explanation: The irregular superlative of good is best. Goodest and most good do not exist, and better compares only two things.

p.text: A bike is slower _____ a car.
p.correction: A bike is slower than a car.
p.explanation: We use than after a comparative adjective like slower to join the two things we compare.

p.text: Mia is as tall _____ her mother now.
p.correction: Mia is as tall as her mother now.
p.explanation: We use as ... as to say two things are equal. The second word must be as, not than.

p.text: My new phone is _____ than my old one.
p.correction: My new phone is bigger than my old one.
p.explanation: Big ends in one vowel and one consonant, so we double the g and add -er: bigger.

p.text: Tom _____ Sam.
p.correction: Tom is older than Sam.
p.explanation: If Sam is younger than Tom, then Tom is older than Sam. Both sentences use than after the comparative.
p.leadInSentence: Sam is younger than Tom.

p.text: This is the most expensive restaurant in the city.
p.correction: This is the most expensive restaurant in the city.
p.explanation: Expensive is a long adjective, so the superlative is the most expensive.

p.text: Your English is more good than mine.
p.correction: Your English is better than mine.
p.explanation: Good has an irregular comparative: better. We never say more good.

p.text: She is as tall than her brother.
p.correction: She is as tall as her brother.
p.explanation: With as ... as, the second word is as, not than. Than is only used after -er or more.

p.text: The train is _____ expensive than the bus.
p.correction: The train is more expensive than the bus.
p.explanation: Expensive is a long adjective, so we use more + adjective + than. Most is a superlative, and much or as cannot be followed by than here.

p.text: Anna's cooking is _____ than mine.
p.correction: Anna's cooking is worse than mine.
p.explanation: The irregular comparative of bad is worse. Worst is a superlative, and more bad and badder do not exist.

p.text: This exam was not as difficult _____ I expected.
p.correction: This exam was not as difficult as I expected.
p.explanation: We use not as ... as to say two things are not equal. The second word is as, not than.

p.text: The book _____ this film.
p.correction: The book is better than this film.
p.explanation: If the film is not as good as the book, then the book is better than the film.
p.leadInSentence: This film is not as good as the book.

p.text: The box _____ for me to lift.
p.correction: The box isn't light enough for me to lift.
p.explanation: Too heavy means not light enough. Enough comes after the adjective: light enough.
p.leadInSentence: The box is too heavy for me to lift.

p.text: I am much _____ now than I was last year.
p.correction: I am much happier now than I was last year.
p.explanation: Happy ends in a consonant plus y, so y changes to i and we add -er: happier.

p.text: The more you practise, the best you become.
p.correction: The more you practise, the better you become.
p.explanation: In this structure both parts need a comparative: the more ..., the better. Best is a superlative.

p.text: Living in a city is far more expensive than living in a village.
p.correction: Living in a city is far more expensive than living in a village.
p.explanation: Far can go before a comparative to mean much: far more expensive.

p.text: This is one of the most interesting books I have ever read.
p.correction: This is one of the most interesting books I have ever read.
p.explanation: After one of the + superlative we use a plural noun: one of the most interesting books.
p.grammarPhrase: one of the most interesting books

p.text: Tokyo is _____ the biggest cities in the world.
p.correction: Tokyo is one of the biggest cities in the world.
p.explanation: We say one of the + superlative + plural noun. One from, the one of and of one are not natural English.

p.text: This phone is a bit _____ than the old one, and it is much faster.
p.correction: This phone is a bit cheaper than the old one, and it is much faster.
p.explanation: Cheap is a short adjective, so the comparative is cheaper. Cheapest is a superlative and more cheap is incorrect.

p.text: My train journey takes twice _____ long as yours.
p.correction: My train journey takes twice as long as yours.
p.explanation: We use twice as + adjective + as to compare amounts. The first gap here is the first as.

p.text: The _____ people there are, the noisier the room gets.
p.correction: The more people there are, the noisier the room gets.
p.explanation: With the + comparative, the + comparative we need more here: the more people, the noisier.

p.text: This is the most _____ chair in the whole shop.
p.correction: This is the most comfortable chair in the whole shop.
p.explanation: After most we need an adjective, so COMFORT becomes comfortable.

p.text: Maya _____ in our team.
p.correction: Maya is the fastest runner in our team.
p.explanation: If nobody runs as fast as Maya, she is the fastest runner. Runs the fastest also keeps the same meaning.
p.leadInSentence: Nobody in our team runs as fast as Maya.

p.text: Their new flat is nowhere near as spacious than the old one.
p.correction: Their new flat is nowhere near as spacious as the old one.
p.explanation: Nowhere near as ... is followed by as, not than.

p.text: The harder the exam was, the more nervous we all felt.
p.correction: The harder the exam was, the more nervous we all felt.
p.explanation: Both parts of this structure use the + comparative: the harder, the more nervous.

p.text: He is by far the more talented player in the squad.
p.correction: He is by far the most talented player in the squad.
p.explanation: A squad has many players, so we need the superlative: the most talented. The more talented is used only between two.

p.text: She drives a bit more carefully than she used to.
p.correction: She drives a bit more carefully than she used to.
p.explanation: Carefully is an adverb, so we use more carefully. A bit makes the difference small.

p.text: The film was _____ boring that we left halfway through.
p.correction: The film was so boring that we left halfway through.
p.explanation: We use so + adjective + that to show result. Such needs a noun, and too or very cannot be followed by that here.

p.text: It was _____ a gripping novel that I read it in one night.
p.correction: It was such a gripping novel that I read it in one night.
p.explanation: We use such a + adjective + noun + that. So cannot be used before a/an + adjective.

p.text: Flights are getting _____ expensive every year.
p.correction: Flights are getting increasingly expensive every year.
p.explanation: The word modifies the adjective expensive, so we need an adverb: increasingly.

p.text: She was the most _____ candidate we interviewed.
p.correction: She was the most impressive candidate we interviewed.
p.explanation: After most we need an adjective, so IMPRESS becomes impressive.

p.text: This is _____ I have ever read.
p.correction: This is the most moving book I have ever read.
p.explanation: Never ... a more moving book than this means the same as the most moving book ever. We use the present perfect with ever.
p.leadInSentence: I have never read a more moving book than this one.

p.text: Our profits are only half as high than they were last year.
p.correction: Our profits are only half as high as they were last year.
p.explanation: Multiplier expressions use as ... as: half as high as. Than does not follow as.

p.text: The more convincingly she argued, the less inclined the board was to object.
p.correction: The more convincingly she argued, the less inclined the board was to object.
p.explanation: Both clauses use the + comparative: the more convincingly, the less inclined.

p.text: Far from being the least talented, she was arguably the most gifted student of her year.
p.correction: Far from being the least talented, she was arguably the most gifted student of her year.
p.explanation: Both the least talented and the most gifted are correct superlatives followed by of her year.

p.text: The negotiations proved _____ more difficult than the mediators had anticipated.
p.correction: The negotiations proved far more difficult than the mediators had anticipated.
p.explanation: Far can intensify a comparative: far more difficult. Very, so and most cannot be used before more.

p.text: The sooner you submit the draft, _____ time we will have to revise it.
p.correction: The sooner you submit the draft, the more time we will have to revise it.
p.explanation: The structure is the + comparative, the + comparative: the sooner ..., the more time. The other options break this pattern.

p.text: No sooner had we sat down _____ the fire alarm went off.
p.correction: No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm went off.
p.explanation: No sooner is a comparative form and takes than, not when.

p.text: She is, by _____, the most gifted pianist in the school.
p.correction: She is, by far, the most gifted pianist in the school.
p.explanation: By far is used before a superlative to mean much more than the rest.

p.text: Her latest film is by far her most _____ work to date.
p.correction: Her latest film is by far her most ambitious work to date.
p.explanation: After most we need an adjective, so AMBITION becomes ambitious.

p.text: I have never managed a more challenging project _____.
p.correction: I have never managed a more challenging project than this one.
p.explanation: If this is the most challenging project, I have never managed a more challenging one than this.
p.leadInSentence: This is the most challenging project I have ever managed.

p.text: The situation, as it turned out, was far more graver than the ministers had admitted.
p.correction: The situation, as it turned out, was far graver than the ministers had admitted.
p.explanation: Graver is already a comparative, so we cannot add more.

p.text: The older he grew, the more he became tolerant of other people's flaws.
p.correction: The older he grew, the more tolerant he became of other people's flaws.
p.explanation: In the + comparative structure, the comparative phrase comes first: the more tolerant he became.

p.text: The less said about last night's performance, the better.
p.correction: The less said about last night's performance, the better.
p.explanation: This is a fixed pattern: the less said, the better.

p.text: Not even the most seasoned diplomats were any the wiser about the ministers' true intentions.
p.correction: Not even the most seasoned diplomats were any the wiser about the ministers' true intentions.
p.explanation: Any the wiser means no better informed. The most seasoned is a correct superlative.

p.text: The new policy is, if anything, _____ than the one it replaced.
p.correction: The new policy is, if anything, more restrictive than the one it replaced.
p.explanation: Than needs a comparative: more restrictive. The more, most and as restrictive do not go with than.

p.text: She is nowhere _____ as confident as she appears.
p.correction: She is nowhere near as confident as she appears.
p.explanation: Nowhere near as ... as means not at all as. Nowhere nearly is also heard.

p.text: The new rules are _____ more lenient than the old ones.
p.correction: The new rules are surprisingly more lenient than the old ones.
p.explanation: The word modifies the adjective more lenient, so we need an adverb: surprisingly.

p.text: The play was _____ the reviews had claimed.
p.correction: The play was nowhere near as good as the reviews had claimed.
p.explanation: Not nearly as good as and nowhere near as good as both mean much worse than.
p.leadInSentence: The play was not nearly as good as the reviews had claimed.

p.text: The new stadium holds _____ the old one did.
p.correction: The new stadium holds twice as many people as the old one did.
p.explanation: 40,000 is double 20,000, so the new stadium holds twice as many people as the old one did.
p.leadInSentence: The new stadium holds 40,000 people, and the old one held 20,000.

p.text: She enjoys playing tennis after school.
p.correction: She enjoys playing tennis after school.
p.explanation: After enjoy we use the -ing form of the verb.

p.text: My brother wants play football today.
p.correction: My brother wants to play football today.
p.explanation: After want we need to + verb.

p.text: Tom can swim very fast.
p.correction: Tom can swim very fast.
p.explanation: After can we use the bare infinitive (swim), with no s.

p.text: I want _____ a new bike for my birthday.
p.correction: I want to have a new bike for my birthday.
p.explanation: Want is followed by to + verb. We do not use -ing or a bare verb after want.

p.text: We enjoy _____ in the park on Sundays.
p.correction: We enjoy walking in the park on Sundays.
p.explanation: Enjoy is followed by the -ing form. We do not say enjoy to walk.

p.text: I would like _____ drink some water, please.
p.correction: I would like to drink some water, please.
p.explanation: Would like is followed by to + verb.

p.text: He enjoys _____ football with his friends.
p.correction: He enjoys playing football with his friends.
p.explanation: Enjoy is followed by the -ing form, so the verb must end in -ing.

p.text: She enjoys _____ in the sea every summer.
p.correction: She enjoys swimming in the sea every summer.
p.explanation: After enjoy we use the -ing form. Swim doubles the m before -ing.

p.text: Jack _____ ride a horse.
p.correction: Jack knows how to ride a horse.
p.explanation: Knows how to + verb means the same as can + verb.
p.leadInSentence: Jack can ride a horse.

p.text: He decided to stay at home because of the rain.
p.correction: He decided to stay at home because of the rain.
p.explanation: Decide is followed by to + verb.

p.text: We avoid to walk home alone at night.
p.correction: We avoid walking home alone at night.
p.explanation: Avoid is followed by the -ing form, not to + verb.

p.text: I'm interested in learning Spanish this year.
p.correction: I'm interested in learning Spanish this year.
p.explanation: After a preposition such as in, we use the -ing form.

p.text: My little brother is afraid of _____ in the dark.
p.correction: My little brother is afraid of being in the dark.
p.explanation: After the preposition of we use the -ing form.

p.text: We hope _____ you at the party on Friday.
p.correction: We hope to see you at the party on Friday.
p.explanation: Hope is followed by to + verb, not -ing.

p.text: Thanks for _____ me with my homework.
p.correction: Thanks for helping me with my homework.
p.explanation: After the preposition for we use the -ing form of the verb.

p.text: I forgot _____ lock the door, so someone walked in.
p.correction: I forgot to lock the door, so someone walked in.
p.explanation: Forget to + verb means we did not do the thing we had to do.

p.text: My favourite hobby is _____ old stamps.
p.correction: My favourite hobby is collecting old stamps.
p.explanation: After is we can use a gerund as a noun, so the -ing form fits.

p.text: How _____ a picnic?
p.correction: How about having a picnic?
p.explanation: How about is followed by the -ing form to make a suggestion.
p.leadInSentence: Why don't we have a picnic?

p.text: I'm looking forward to meeting your parents next week.
p.correction: I'm looking forward to meeting your parents next week.
p.explanation: In look forward to, the word to is a preposition, so we use -ing.

p.text: She's used to get up early every day.
p.correction: She's used to getting up early every day.
p.explanation: Be used to is followed by -ing because to is a preposition.
p.mistakeType: base verb after be used to

p.text: My teacher made us to rewrite the essay.
p.correction: My teacher made us rewrite the essay.
p.explanation: After make + object we use the bare infinitive, without to, in active sentences.

p.text: The manager persuaded me _____ the job offer.
p.correction: The manager persuaded me to accept the job offer.
p.explanation: Persuade + object is followed by to + verb.

p.text: Remember _____ buy some milk on your way home.
p.correction: Remember to buy some milk on your way home.
p.explanation: Remember to + verb means do not forget to do something.

p.text: He insisted on _____ for the meal, even though we offered.
p.correction: He insisted on paying for the meal, even though we offered.
p.explanation: Insist on is followed by the -ing form because on is a preposition.

p.text: Anna _____ phone the dentist.
p.correction: Anna reminded me to phone the dentist.
p.explanation: Remind + object + to + verb reports a request to remember something.
p.leadInSentence: Anna said to me, "Don't forget to phone the dentist."

p.text: I _____ to my parents.
p.correction: I regret lying to my parents.
p.explanation: Regret + -ing talks about being sorry for something we did in the past.
p.leadInSentence: I'm sorry I lied to my parents.

p.text: He is afraid of _____ in front of a large audience.
p.correction: He is afraid of singing in front of a large audience.
p.explanation: After the preposition of we use the -ing form of the verb.

p.text: He admitted having copied the answers from a classmate.
p.correction: He admitted having copied the answers from a classmate.
p.explanation: Admit is followed by -ing; having + past participle shows the copying happened earlier.

p.text: I'd rather to stay at home than go to the party.
p.correction: I'd rather stay at home than go to the party.
p.explanation: After would rather we use the bare infinitive, without to.

p.text: He resented to be told what to do.
p.correction: He resented being told what to do.
p.explanation: Resent is followed by the -ing form; here the passive gerund being told is needed.

p.text: She's proud of _____ chosen to lead the team.
p.correction: She's proud of being chosen to lead the team.
p.explanation: After the preposition of we need an -ing form, and being + past participle makes it passive.

p.text: You'd better _____ an umbrella; it looks like rain.
p.correction: You'd better take an umbrella; it looks like rain.
p.explanation: Had better is followed by the bare infinitive.

p.text: She can't help _____ nervous before every exam.
p.correction: She can't help feeling nervous before every exam.
p.explanation: Can't help is followed by the -ing form and means she cannot stop herself.

p.text: There is _____ with him.
p.correction: There is no point in arguing with him.
p.explanation: There is no point in is followed by the -ing form.
p.leadInSentence: It is pointless to argue with him.

p.text: The council has no intention of _____ the narrow road.
p.correction: The council has no intention of widening the narrow road.
p.explanation: After the preposition of we use the -ing form; wide becomes widen, then widening.

p.text: The teacher insists on _____ every student fairly.
p.correction: The teacher insists on treating every student fairly.
p.explanation: Insist on is followed by the -ing form.

p.text: Not having been informed of the changes, she turned up at the old venue.
p.correction: Not having been informed of the changes, she turned up at the old venue.
p.explanation: Not having been informed is a negative perfect passive participle clause giving the reason.

p.text: She resents being not invited to the ceremony.
p.correction: She resents not being invited to the ceremony.
p.explanation: In a negative gerund, not comes before being: not being invited.
p.mistakeType: wrong word order in negative gerund

p.text: He would sooner resign than apologise publicly.
p.correction: He would sooner resign than apologise publicly.
p.explanation: Would sooner is followed by the bare infinitive, and so is the verb after than.

p.text: I would rather to have been told earlier.
p.correction: I would rather have been told earlier.
p.explanation: Would rather is followed by the bare infinitive; the perfect form is have been told.

p.text: Nobody objected to _____ the schedule revised.
p.correction: Nobody objected to having the schedule revised.
p.explanation: In object to, the word to is a preposition, so we need the -ing form.

p.text: It's no use _____ over spilt milk.
p.correction: It's no use crying over spilt milk.
p.explanation: It's no use is followed by the -ing form; the idiom means there is no point regretting the past.

p.text: I do not _____ about the new rules.
p.correction: I do not remember being told about the new rules.
p.explanation: Remember + -ing talks about a memory of a past event; being told is the passive gerund.
p.leadInSentence: I do not remember that anyone told me about the new rules.

p.text: She _____ pay the fine despite her protests.
p.correction: She was made to pay the fine despite her protests.
p.explanation: After make the bare infinitive is used in the active, but the passive needs to + verb.
p.leadInSentence: They made her pay the fine despite her protests.

p.text: She was accused of deliberately _____ the survey data.
p.correction: She was accused of deliberately falsifying the survey data.
p.explanation: After the preposition of we use the -ing form; the verb from false is falsify.

p.text: The senator is rumoured to have been negotiating in secret for months.
p.correction: The senator is rumoured to have been negotiating in secret for months.
p.explanation: After is rumoured we use a perfect infinitive; to have been negotiating shows an action over time before now.

p.text: Not for a moment did he contemplate abandoning the project.
p.correction: Not for a moment did he contemplate abandoning the project.
p.explanation: Contemplate is followed by the -ing form.

p.text: She would sooner to resign than compromise her principles.
p.correction: She would sooner resign than compromise her principles.
p.explanation: Would sooner is followed by the bare infinitive, without to.

p.text: The proposal is not worth to discuss at length.
p.correction: The proposal is not worth discussing at length.
p.explanation: Worth is followed by the -ing form.

p.text: The artist is believed _____ working on a mural when she died.
p.correction: The artist is believed to have been working on a mural when she died.
p.explanation: The working happened before now, so we need the perfect infinitive to have been. To be would refer to the present.

p.text: I distinctly remember _____ the oven off before leaving, so I can't think what happened.
p.correction: I distinctly remember turning the oven off before leaving, so I can't think what happened.
p.explanation: Remember + -ing is a memory of a past action. Remember to turn would mean not forgetting to do it.

p.text: Far from _____ embarrassed by the mistake, he laughed it off.
p.correction: Far from being embarrassed by the mistake, he laughed it off.
p.explanation: Far from is a preposition phrase, so it is followed by an -ing form.

p.text: The CEO _____ been selling shares in secret.
p.correction: The CEO is said to have been selling shares in secret.
p.explanation: We can report this with is said + perfect infinitive to show an earlier or ongoing action.
p.grammarPhrase: is said to have been selling
p.leadInSentence: It is said that the CEO has been selling shares in secret.

p.text: She resented being _____ as the junior partner in the firm.
p.correction: She resented being portrayed as the junior partner in the firm.
p.explanation: After being we need a past participle for the passive gerund.
p.grammarPhrase: being portrayed as the junior partner

p.text: The windows are clean every Friday by the caretaker.
p.correction: The windows are cleaned every Friday by the caretaker.
p.explanation: The passive needs be + past participle, so we say 'are cleaned'. 'Clean' is an adjective or base verb here.

p.text: This cake was made by my grandmother last weekend.
p.correction: This cake was made by my grandmother last weekend.
p.explanation: The past simple passive is was/were + past participle, and 'by' introduces the person who did the action.

p.text: The new stadium has been build near the river.
p.correction: The new stadium has been built near the river.
p.explanation: The present perfect passive is has/have been + past participle. The participle of 'build' is 'built', not 'build'.

p.text: My bike was stole outside the library yesterday.
p.correction: My bike was stolen outside the library yesterday.
p.explanation: After 'was' in a passive sentence we need the past participle 'stolen', not the past simple 'stole'.

p.text: I had my laptop repaired at the shop on Baker Street.
p.correction: I had my laptop repaired at the shop on Baker Street.
p.explanation: 'Have + object + past participle' means someone else did the job for you.

p.text: Mobile phones must not be use during the exam.
p.correction: Mobile phones must not be used during the exam.
p.explanation: A modal passive is modal + be + past participle, so we need 'be used'.

p.text: Two of the players got injured during the first half.
p.correction: Two of the players got injured during the first half.
p.explanation: 'Get' + past participle can replace 'be' in informal passives, especially for unplanned events.

p.text: The company is said to have lost millions of pounds last year.
p.correction: The company is said to have lost millions of pounds last year.
p.explanation: 'Is said to have + past participle' reports a belief about something that happened earlier.

p.text: He is said that he has retired and moved abroad.
p.correction: It is said that he has retired and moved abroad.
p.explanation: With 'that' + clause we use the empty subject 'It'. We could also say 'He is said to have retired'.

p.text: The suspect denied having been informed of his rights before questioning.
p.correction: The suspect denied having been informed of his rights before questioning.
p.explanation: 'Having been + past participle' is the perfect gerund passive, used after verbs like 'deny' for an earlier event.

p.text: Not until the report had been leaked was the board forced to act.
p.correction: Not until the report had been leaked was the board forced to act.
p.explanation: After 'Not until' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: 'was the board forced'.

p.text: Only after the data had been verified the findings were published.
p.correction: Only after the data had been verified were the findings published.
p.explanation: After 'Only after ...' at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary goes before the subject: 'were the findings published'.

p.text: The manuscript is thought to have copied by monks in the ninth century.
p.correction: The manuscript is thought to have been copied by monks in the ninth century.
p.explanation: The manuscript did not copy itself, so we need the perfect passive infinitive 'to have been copied'.

p.text: Tom said that he was tired after the long walk.
p.correction: Tom said that he was tired after the long walk.
p.explanation: Direct speech 'I am tired' becomes 'he was tired' in reported speech (backshift).

p.text: The waiter told to us that the kitchen was closed.
p.correction: The waiter told us that the kitchen was closed.
p.explanation: 'Tell' takes the person directly ('told us') with no 'to'. We say 'said to us' but 'told us'.

p.text: She asked me whether I wanted to join the choir.
p.correction: She asked me whether I wanted to join the choir.
p.explanation: Reported yes/no questions use if/whether with statement word order and backshift.

p.text: The coach told us run ten laps before breakfast.
p.correction: The coach told us to run ten laps before breakfast.
p.explanation: Reported commands use 'told + person + to + base verb'.

p.text: My brother suggested taking the night bus to save money.
p.correction: My brother suggested taking the night bus to save money.
p.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by an -ing form (or a that-clause), not by a to-infinitive.

p.text: She denied to have broken the vase in the hallway.
p.correction: She denied having broken the vase in the hallway.
p.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by an -ing form, so we say 'denied having broken' (or 'denied breaking').

p.text: He asked if could he borrow my charger that evening.
p.correction: He asked if he could borrow my charger that evening.
p.explanation: In reported questions the subject comes before the verb, as in a statement: 'he could borrow'.
p.mistakeType: question word order in reported question

p.text: The mayor apologised for not having responded to residents' complaints sooner.
p.correction: The mayor apologised for not having responded to residents' complaints sooner.
p.explanation: 'Apologise' takes 'for' + an -ing form; 'not having responded' refers to something earlier.

p.text: The CEO refused admitting responsibility for the failed launch.
p.correction: The CEO refused to admit responsibility for the failed launch.
p.explanation: 'Refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form.

p.text: She wondered whether the findings would still hold the following year.
p.correction: She wondered whether the findings would still hold the following year.
p.explanation: Reported questions keep statement word order, and 'next year' becomes 'the following year'.

p.text: He claimed to have been misquoted, insisting that he had never made such remarks.
p.correction: He claimed to have been misquoted, insisting that he had never made such remarks.
p.explanation: 'Claim' can take a perfect infinitive; 'had never made' is the backshifted past perfect.

p.text: The witness could not recall whether had the defendant been present.
p.correction: The witness could not recall whether the defendant had been present.
p.explanation: After 'whether' a reported question uses statement order: 'the defendant had been'.
p.mistakeType: question word order in reported question

p.text: Asked what did she intend to do next, the senator declined to comment.
p.correction: Asked what she intended to do next, the senator declined to comment.
p.explanation: An embedded question uses statement order and no 'did': 'what she intended'.
p.mistakeType: question word order in reported question

p.text: Please switch off your phone in the cinema.
p.correction: Please switch off your phone in the cinema.
p.explanation: 'Switch off' means stop a machine working.

p.text: I picked up it from the floor.
p.correction: I picked it up from the floor.
p.explanation: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object goes between the verb and the particle: 'picked it up'.

p.text: Please turn the music down; the baby is sleeping.
p.correction: Please turn the music down; the baby is sleeping.
p.explanation: 'Turn down' means lower the volume, and the noun object can go in the middle.

p.text: The plane took up at nine and landed at noon.
p.correction: The plane took off at nine and landed at noon.
p.explanation: When a plane leaves the ground, we say it 'takes off'. 'Take up' means start a hobby or use space.

p.text: We ran out of milk, so I went to the shop.
p.correction: We ran out of milk, so I went to the shop.
p.explanation: 'Run out of' is a three-part verb meaning have no more of something.

p.text: The teacher handed out them to the class.
p.correction: The teacher handed them out to the class.
p.explanation: A pronoun object must come between the verb and particle of a separable verb: 'handed them out'.

p.text: She takes after her father; they both love painting.
p.correction: She takes after her father; they both love painting.
p.explanation: 'Take after' means be similar to a family member, and the object follows the particle.

p.text: I can't put up it any longer; the noise is unbearable.
p.correction: I can't put up with it any longer; the noise is unbearable.
p.explanation: 'Put up with' is a three-part verb meaning tolerate, and its object comes after 'with'.

p.text: The negotiations broke down after both sides refused to compromise.
p.correction: The negotiations broke down after both sides refused to compromise.
p.explanation: 'Break down' means fail or stop working, and it takes no object.

p.text: The negotiators have come up a compromise at last.
p.correction: The negotiators have come up with a compromise at last.
p.explanation: 'Come up with' means think of an idea or solution, so it needs 'with' before its object.

p.text: The scandal has blown over, but the damage to his reputation lingers.
p.correction: The scandal has blown over, but the damage to his reputation lingers.
p.explanation: 'Blow over' means a problem gradually stops being talked about.

p.text: The factory had to lay off two hundred workers when orders dried on.
p.correction: The factory had to lay off two hundred workers when orders dried up.
p.explanation: When supply or demand stops completely we say it 'dries up'.

p.text: I'll mull the proposal over and get back to you on Monday.
p.correction: I'll mull the proposal over and get back to you on Monday.
p.explanation: 'Mull over' means think carefully about something, and the noun object can come between verb and particle.

p.text: I'd like to take a shower before dinner.
p.correction: I'd like to take a shower before dinner.
p.explanation: We say 'take a shower', not 'do' or 'make' a shower.

p.text: Let's make a break and have some tea.
p.correction: Let's take a break and have some tea.
p.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'take a break'.

p.text: Heavy traffic made us late for the concert.
p.correction: Heavy traffic made us late for the concert.
p.explanation: We say 'heavy traffic' and 'heavy rain', not 'strong traffic'.

p.text: After a long talk, Omar did a decision about university.
p.correction: After a long talk, Omar made a decision about university.
p.explanation: We 'make' a decision. 'Do' is used for tasks and activities.

p.text: The new law will have a significant impact on small farms.
p.correction: The new law will have a significant impact on small farms.
p.explanation: 'Have an impact on' is the standard collocation, and 'significant' is a common adjective with it.

p.text: After weeks of talks, the two sides finally did an agreement.
p.correction: After weeks of talks, the two sides finally reached an agreement.
p.explanation: We say 'reach an agreement'. 'Do an agreement' is not used in English.

p.text: The minister came under fierce criticism for the delayed response.
p.correction: The minister came under fierce criticism for the delayed response.
p.explanation: 'Fierce criticism' is a natural collocation for very strong disapproval.

p.text: It is too early to take a conclusion from the data.
p.correction: It is too early to draw a conclusion from the data.
p.explanation: We 'draw' a conclusion from evidence. 'Take a conclusion' is not used.

p.text: The findings lend credence to the theory that the climate shifted abruptly.
p.correction: The findings lend credence to the theory that the climate shifted abruptly.
p.explanation: 'Lend credence to' is a formal collocation meaning make something more believable.

p.text: The talks have done little headway since March.
p.correction: The talks have made little headway since March.
p.explanation: 'Headway' collocates with 'make': 'make headway' means progress.

p.text: The company's sudden collapse sent shockwaves through the industry.
p.correction: The company's sudden collapse sent shockwaves through the industry.
p.explanation: 'Send shockwaves through' is a fixed phrase meaning cause a strong shock to a group.

p.text: You mustn't pay to enter the museum; it's free on Sundays.
p.correction: You don't have to pay to enter the museum; it's free on Sundays.
p.explanation: 'Mustn't' means it is forbidden. Here there is simply no need to pay, so we say 'don't have to'.

p.text: That can't be Ana's bag; she took her blue one this morning.
p.correction: That can't be Ana's bag; she took her blue one this morning.
p.explanation: 'Can't be' expresses a strong belief that something is impossible.

p.text: I needn't to have bought so much food; nobody came.
p.correction: I needn't have bought so much food; nobody came.
p.explanation: 'Needn't' is a modal verb, so it is followed by 'have' + past participle without 'to'.

p.text: She must have been exhausted after driving through the night.
p.correction: She must have been exhausted after driving through the night.
p.explanation: 'Must have + past participle' shows a strong conclusion about the past.

p.text: He was lucky to survive; he might be killed in that crash.
p.correction: He was lucky to survive; he might have been killed in that crash.
p.explanation: For a past possibility that did not happen we use 'might have been'. 'Might be' refers to the present or future.

p.text: You needn't have gone to such lengths; a simple note would have sufficed.
p.correction: You needn't have gone to such lengths; a simple note would have sufficed.
p.explanation: 'Needn't have + participle' means you did something that was not necessary.

p.text: Whoever sent the letter must had known his address.
p.correction: Whoever sent the letter must have known his address.
p.explanation: Modals take 'have' + past participle for past deduction, not 'had'.

p.text: By the time the findings are published, we will have been researching this for nearly a decade.
p.correction: By the time the findings are published, we will have been researching this for nearly a decade.
p.explanation: Future perfect continuous shows how long an activity will have lasted by a future point.

p.text: No sooner had she sat down than the phone rings.
p.correction: No sooner had she sat down than the phone rang.
p.explanation: 'No sooner had ... than' describes two past events, so the second verb is in the past simple.

p.text: I'd rather you hadn't mentioned the merger to the press.
p.correction: I'd rather you hadn't mentioned the merger to the press.
p.explanation: 'Would rather' + subject + past perfect expresses regret about what someone did.

p.text: Sam _____ in his bag.
p.correction: Sam has an orange in his bag.
p.explanation: We use 'an' before a singular noun that starts with a vowel sound, such as 'orange'.
p.leadInSentence: Sam has one orange in his bag.

p.text: She goes to the cinema _____.
p.correction: She goes to the cinema twice a month.
p.explanation: We use 'a' with a time word to mean 'per' or 'each': 'twice a month'.
p.leadInSentence: She goes to the cinema two times every month.

p.text: This is _____ beautiful beach I have ever seen.
p.correction: This is the most beautiful beach I have ever seen.
p.explanation: A superlative adjective needs 'the' before it: 'the most beautiful'.
p.leadInSentence: I have never seen a more beautiful beach than this one.

p.text: It was _____ that we left early.
p.correction: It was such a boring film that we left early.
p.explanation: After 'such' we use 'a/an' + adjective + singular noun: 'such a boring film'.
p.leadInSentence: The film was so boring that we left early.

p.text: She was _____ woman to run the company.
p.correction: She was the first woman to run the company.
p.explanation: We use 'the' before ordinal numbers such as 'first', so it is 'the first woman to run the company'.
p.leadInSentence: No woman had run the company before she did.

p.text: On _____, the trip was a success.
p.correction: On the whole, the trip was a success.
p.explanation: 'On the whole' is a fixed phrase meaning 'generally' and it needs 'the'.
p.leadInSentence: Generally speaking, the trip was a success.

p.text: We _____ at eight.
p.correction: We had breakfast at eight.
p.explanation: The natural collocation for meals is 'have breakfast', so in the past it is 'had breakfast'.
p.leadInSentence: We ate breakfast at eight.

p.text: Tom _____ after the rain.
p.correction: Tom caught a cold after the rain.
p.explanation: We say 'catch a cold', and the past form is 'caught'.
p.leadInSentence: Tom got a cold after the rain.

p.text: The concert _____ in the old town hall.
p.correction: The concert took place in the old town hall.
p.explanation: 'Take place' is a fixed collocation meaning 'happen' for planned events.
p.leadInSentence: The concert happened in the old town hall.

p.text: Daniel _____ to repay the loan.
p.correction: Daniel broke his promise to repay the loan.
p.explanation: We 'break' a promise when we do not do what we said, so 'did not keep his promise' = 'broke his promise'.
p.leadInSentence: Daniel did not keep his promise to repay the loan.

p.text: The panel _____ the cost of living when setting salaries.
p.correction: The panel took account of the cost of living when setting salaries.
p.explanation: 'Take account of' (or 'take into account') is the usual collocation meaning 'consider'.
p.leadInSentence: The panel considered the cost of living when setting salaries.

p.text: She _____ by her colleagues.
p.correction: She is held in high regard by her colleagues.
p.explanation: 'Be held in high regard' is a passive collocation meaning 'be greatly respected'.
p.leadInSentence: Her colleagues think very highly of her.

p.text: The manager _____ eye to the late arrivals.
p.correction: The manager turned a blind eye to the late arrivals.
p.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye to' is an idiom meaning to pretend not to see something wrong on purpose.
p.leadInSentence: The manager deliberately ignored the late arrivals.

p.text: It is cold, so _____ your coat.
p.correction: It is cold, so put on your coat.
p.explanation: 'Put on' means to wear something. We can say 'put on your coat'.
p.leadInSentence: It is cold, so wear your coat.

p.text: Sara _____ her little brother after school.
p.correction: Sara looks after her little brother after school.
p.explanation: 'Look after' means 'take care of'. With 'Sara' we need the -s: 'looks after'.
p.leadInSentence: Sara takes care of her little brother after school.

p.text: We have _____ milk.
p.correction: We have run out of milk.
p.explanation: 'Run out of' means to have no more of something. The present perfect needs 'run' (past participle).
p.leadInSentence: We have used all of the milk.

p.text: The company decided _____ the launch until spring.
p.correction: The company decided to put off the launch until spring.
p.explanation: 'Put off' means 'postpone'. After 'decided' we use 'to' + infinitive: 'to put off'.
p.leadInSentence: The company decided to postpone the launch until spring.

p.text: She _____ a clever way to save energy.
p.correction: She came up with a clever way to save energy.
p.explanation: 'Come up with' means to think of an idea. The past simple is 'came up with'.
p.leadInSentence: She thought of a clever way to save energy.

p.text: The merger _____ because the investors withdrew.
p.correction: The merger fell through because the investors withdrew.
p.explanation: 'Fall through' means that a plan or deal fails to happen. The past simple of 'fall' is 'fell'.
p.leadInSentence: The merger failed to happen because the investors withdrew.

p.text: He has _____ for promotion several times.
p.correction: He has been passed over for promotion several times.
p.explanation: 'Pass over' means to ignore someone for promotion. Here it is passive in the present perfect: 'has been passed over'.
p.leadInSentence: Several times the firm has promoted other people instead of him.

p.text: The shop is _____ my house.
p.correction: The shop is close to my house.
p.explanation: 'Close to' means 'not far from'. The preposition after 'close' is 'to'.
p.leadInSentence: The shop is not far from my house.

p.text: Ben _____ football.
p.correction: Ben is interested in football.
p.explanation: We say 'be interested in' something. The preposition is 'in'.
p.leadInSentence: Ben thinks football is interesting.

p.text: _____ Ana's help, we finished early.
p.correction: Thanks to Ana's help, we finished early.
p.explanation: 'Thanks to' means 'because of' and shows a good reason or cause.
p.leadInSentence: Because of Ana's help, we finished early.

p.text: Maya is _____ the ticket sales.
p.correction: Maya is in charge of the ticket sales.
p.explanation: 'Be in charge of' means 'be responsible for'. The fixed phrase ends with 'of'.
p.leadInSentence: Maya is responsible for the ticket sales.

p.text: I am speaking _____ all the staff.
p.correction: I am speaking on behalf of all the staff.
p.explanation: 'On behalf of' means 'as a representative of'. It is always followed by 'of'.
p.leadInSentence: I am speaking for all the staff.

p.text: _____ heavy snow, the match will be cancelled.
p.correction: In the event of heavy snow, the match will be cancelled.
p.explanation: 'In the event of' is a formal phrase meaning 'if there is'. It is followed by a noun.
p.leadInSentence: In case of heavy snow, the match will be cancelled.

p.text: His views on the budget _____ those of the board.
p.correction: His views on the budget are at odds with those of the board.
p.explanation: 'Be at odds with' means to disagree with or conflict with. It is a fixed phrase with 'at' and 'with'.
p.leadInSentence: His views on the budget conflict with those of the board.

p.text: The hotel staff were extremely _____ and carried our bags to the room.
p.correction: The hotel staff were extremely helpful and carried our bags to the room.
p.explanation: After 'extremely' we need an adjective describing the staff, so HELP becomes 'helpful'.

p.text: The teacher told us to be _____ with our spelling in the exam.
p.correction: The teacher told us to be careful with our spelling in the exam.
p.explanation: After 'be' we need an adjective, so CARE becomes 'careful'.

p.text: You really should be more _____ when you cross a busy road.
p.correction: You really should be more cautious when you cross a busy road.
p.explanation: After 'more' and 'be' we need an adjective, so CAUTION becomes 'cautious'.

p.text: The new rules apply to all employees _____ of their position.
p.correction: The new rules apply to all employees regardless of their position.
p.explanation: 'Regardless of' means 'without being affected by'. The word is 'regardless'.

p.text: The spokesman _____ denied that the company had misled its customers.
p.correction: The spokesman firmly denied that the company had misled its customers.
p.explanation: An adverb is needed to describe the verb 'denied', so FIRM becomes 'firmly'.

p.text: It is highly _____ that the meeting will finish before noon, as twenty items are still to be discussed.
p.correction: It is highly unlikely that the meeting will finish before noon, as twenty items are still to be discussed.
p.explanation: Twenty items remain, so finishing early is not probable. We need the negative adjective 'unlikely'.

p.text: The _____ of the new bridge was delayed by bad weather.
p.correction: The construction of the new bridge was delayed by bad weather.
p.explanation: After 'The' we need a noun, so CONSTRUCT becomes 'construction'.

p.text: Her _____ to give up, even after three failures, impressed the judges.
p.correction: Her refusal to give up, even after three failures, impressed the judges.
p.explanation: After 'Her' we need a noun, so REFUSE becomes 'refusal'.

p.text: The witness's version of events was so _____ that the judge ordered a fresh hearing.
p.correction: The witness's version of events was so inconsistent that the judge ordered a fresh hearing.
p.explanation: The judge ordered a new hearing, so the account must have contradicted itself. We need the negative 'inconsistent'.

p.text: The _____ of the scheme succeeding depends largely on public support.
p.correction: The likelihood of the scheme succeeding depends largely on public support.
p.explanation: After 'The' and before 'of' we need a noun, so LIKELY becomes 'likelihood'.

p.text: The two proposals are _____ different, so they cannot be compared directly.
p.correction: The two proposals are fundamentally different, so they cannot be compared directly.
p.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify the adjective 'different', so FUNDAMENTAL becomes 'fundamentally'.

p.text: The sheer _____ of the desert left the explorers speechless.
p.correction: The sheer vastness of the desert left the explorers speechless.
p.explanation: After 'sheer' and before 'of' we need a noun, so VAST becomes 'vastness'.

p.text: She is _____ the most capable candidate we have ever interviewed.
p.correction: She is unquestionably the most capable candidate we have ever interviewed.
p.explanation: We need an adverb meaning 'without doubt' before 'the most capable': 'unquestionably'.

p.text: Even when shown the evidence, the authors remained _____ to admit that some figures might have been exaggerated.
p.correction: Even when shown the evidence, the authors remained unwilling to admit that some figures might have been exaggerated.
p.explanation: 'Even when shown the evidence' signals refusal, so we need the negative 'unwilling'.

p.text: The company went ahead in _____ of the regulator's repeated warnings.
p.correction: The company went ahead in defiance of the regulator's repeated warnings.
p.explanation: After 'in' and before 'of' we need a noun: 'in defiance of' means openly ignoring a rule or warning.

p.text: _____ the storm, the flight would have landed on time.
p.correction: Had it not been for the storm, the flight would have landed on time.
p.explanation: 'Had it not been for' is the inverted third conditional (= 'If it had not been for'). It matches 'would have landed'. 'Were it not for' is for present situations, and the other options are not grammatical.

p.text: If she _____ the job in Berlin last year, she would be living there now.
p.correction: If she had accepted the job in Berlin last year, she would be living there now.
p.explanation: A mixed conditional with a past condition and present result uses 'if' + past perfect, then 'would' + infinitive. 'Would' is not used in the 'if' clause.

p.text: By the time the conference ends, the delegates _____ for nearly twelve hours.
p.correction: By the time the conference ends, the delegates will have been negotiating for nearly twelve hours.
p.explanation: 'By the time ... ends' plus a duration ('for twelve hours') needs the future perfect continuous. 'Have been negotiating' does not fit a future point, and 'will negotiate' ignores the duration.

p.text: It is high time the government _____ action on housing costs.
p.correction: It is high time the government took action on housing costs.
p.explanation: After 'It is high time' we use the past simple to talk about the present or future. 'Takes' and 'will take' are wrong, and 'to take' cannot follow a clause subject.

p.text: You _____ have rushed; the train was delayed by an hour.
p.correction: You needn't have rushed; the train was delayed by an hour.
p.explanation: 'Needn't have' + past participle means you did something that was not necessary. 'Mustn't have' and 'can't have' express wrong kinds of meaning here.

p.text: The new policy is incompatible _____ the values our school promotes.
p.correction: The new policy is incompatible with the values our school promotes.
p.explanation: The adjective 'incompatible' is followed by 'with'. The other prepositions are not used after it.

p.text: Contrary _____ popular belief, bats are not blind.
p.correction: Contrary to popular belief, bats are not blind.
p.explanation: 'Contrary to' is a fixed phrase meaning 'opposite to'. 'With', 'of' and 'for' do not form this phrase.

p.text: He was _____ last person I would have expected to complain.
p.correction: He was the last person I would have expected to complain.
p.explanation: 'The last person' is a fixed pattern meaning the least likely person. 'A last' or 'one last' would change the meaning.

p.text: She denied _____ the confidential file, although the footage suggested otherwise.
p.correction: She denied having leaked the confidential file, although the footage suggested otherwise.
p.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund (here the perfect gerund 'having leaked') for an earlier action. It cannot be followed by a 'to' infinitive.

p.text: Hardly _____ she stepped off the plane when the rain began.
p.correction: Hardly had she stepped off the plane when the rain began.
p.explanation: After 'Hardly' we use inversion and the past perfect: 'Hardly had she stepped off ... when ...'.

p.text: Little did she suspect that the quiet village _____ soon become famous.
p.correction: Little did she suspect that the quiet village would soon become famous.
p.explanation: 'Would' expresses the future seen from a past moment, here after the inverted 'Little did she suspect'.
p.subtype: would as future in the past

p.text: You _____ better double-check the figures before submitting the report.
p.correction: You had better double-check the figures before submitting the report.
p.explanation: 'Had better' + infinitive without 'to' gives strong advice. The word needed is 'had'.

p.text: The fragile ceasefire is on the verge _____ collapse.
p.correction: The fragile ceasefire is on the verge of collapse.
p.explanation: 'On the verge of' is a fixed phrase meaning 'very close to'. It is followed by 'of'.

p.text: It is _____ great shame that so many old buildings are being demolished.
p.correction: It is a great shame that so many old buildings are being demolished.
p.explanation: 'Shame' is used in the pattern 'It is a (great) shame that ...', which needs the indefinite article 'a'.

p.text: Such was _____ force of the impact that every window in the street shattered.
p.correction: Such was the force of the impact that every window in the street shattered.
p.explanation: In 'Such was the force of the impact that ...' the noun is made specific by 'of the impact', so it needs 'the'.

p.text: The minister is said _____ be considering resignation after the report.
p.correction: The minister is said to be considering resignation after the report.
p.explanation: 'Be said to' + infinitive is a common impersonal reporting structure. The missing word is 'to'.

p.text: _____ you require further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact our help desk.
p.correction: Should you require further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact our help desk.
p.explanation: 'Should + subject + verb' replaces 'If you require' in formal, polite conditionals.

p.text: The shop who sells cheap shoes is near the park.
p.correction: The shop which sells cheap shoes is near the park.
p.explanation: We use 'which' (or 'that') for things and places. 'Who' is only for people.

p.text: The teacher who teaches us maths is very kind.
p.correction: The teacher who teaches us maths is very kind.
p.explanation: 'Teacher' is a person, so 'who' is correct.

p.text: I like the book what you gave me.
p.correction: I like the book that you gave me.
p.explanation: 'What' cannot join a clause to a noun. Use 'that' or 'which' for a thing.

p.text: Tom has a sister who lives in Spain.
p.correction: Tom has a sister who lives in Spain.
p.explanation: 'Sister' is a person, so we use 'who'.

p.text: A baker is a person _____ makes bread.
p.correction: A baker is a person who makes bread.
p.explanation: 'Person' needs 'who'. 'Which' is for things, 'where' is for places and 'whose' shows possession.

p.text: This is the shop _____ I buy my shoes.
p.correction: This is the shop where I buy my shoes.
p.explanation: 'Where' refers to a place and the clause has its own subject (I). 'Who' is for people, and 'which' would need a preposition ('in which').

p.text: The man _____ lives next door has a big dog.
p.correction: The man who lives next door has a big dog.
p.explanation: 'Man' is a person, so 'who' fits ('that' is also possible).

p.text: I have a bag _____ is very old.
p.correction: I have a bag which is very old.
p.explanation: 'Bag' is a thing, so we use 'which' or 'that'.

p.text: My brother is a great _____ who plays in a band.
p.correction: My brother is a great musician who plays in a band.
p.explanation: After 'a great' we need a noun for a person; 'who plays' describes that person.

p.text: The boy which won the race is my cousin.
p.correction: The boy who won the race is my cousin.
p.explanation: 'Boy' is a person, so we use 'who' (or 'that'), not 'which'.

p.text: My aunt, who lives in Leeds, is visiting us on Saturday.
p.correction: My aunt, who lives in Leeds, is visiting us on Saturday.
p.explanation: The extra information is between commas and 'who' refers to a person, so this is correct.

p.text: The man who he lives next door is a doctor.
p.correction: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
p.explanation: 'Who' is already the subject of 'lives', so we do not add 'he'.

p.text: That is the girl _____ bike was stolen.
p.correction: That is the girl whose bike was stolen.
p.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession (the girl's bike). The other words cannot be followed directly by a noun like this.

p.text: Do you remember the café _____ we had lunch last week?
p.correction: Do you remember the café where we had lunch last week?
p.explanation: 'Where' replaces 'in the cafe' and joins the place to the clause.

p.text: I don't know anyone _____ plays chess.
p.correction: I don't know anyone who plays chess.
p.explanation: 'Anyone' refers to a person and the gap is the subject, so 'who' (or 'that') is needed.

p.text: We stayed in a hotel _____.
p.correction: We stayed in a hotel which was near the beach.
p.explanation: 'Which' replaces 'it' and joins the two sentences.
p.grammarPhrase: hotel which was near the beach
p.leadInSentence: We stayed in a hotel. It was near the beach.

p.text: This is the girl _____ my class.
p.correction: This is the girl whose brother is in my class.
p.explanation: 'Whose' replaces 'her' to show whose brother it is.
p.leadInSentence: This is the girl. Her brother is in my class.

p.text: My neighbour, who is a very _____ man, often carries our shopping.
p.correction: My neighbour, who is a very helpful man, often carries our shopping.
p.explanation: After 'very' and before 'man' we need an adjective: 'helpful'.
p.grammarPhrase: who is a very helpful man

p.text: My phone, that I bought last year, has stopped working.
p.correction: My phone, which I bought last year, has stopped working.
p.explanation: We cannot use 'that' in a non-defining clause (one with commas). Use 'which'.

p.text: The reason why she left early was never explained.
p.correction: The reason why she left early was never explained.
p.explanation: 'Why' can follow 'reason' to introduce the explanation.

p.text: This is the village where I was born in.
p.correction: This is the village where I was born.
p.explanation: 'Where' already means 'in which', so the extra 'in' is wrong.

p.text: My grandfather, _____ is eighty, still plays tennis.
p.correction: My grandfather, who is eighty, still plays tennis.
p.explanation: The clause between commas is non-defining, so 'that' is not possible. 'Who' is used for a person, and 'which' is for things.

p.text: The hotel in _____ we stayed was close to the sea.
p.correction: The hotel in which we stayed was close to the sea.
p.explanation: After a preposition we use 'which' for things. We cannot use 'that' or 'where' directly after 'in'.

p.text: She is the neighbour to _____ I gave my spare key.
p.correction: She is the neighbour to whom I gave my spare key.
p.explanation: After a preposition we use 'whom' for a person, not 'who'.

p.text: The woman _____ at the station was very kind.
p.correction: The woman to whom I spoke at the station was very kind.
p.explanation: 'Whom' replaces 'her' as the object of 'spoke to'; the preposition comes before it in formal style.
p.leadInSentence: The woman was very kind. I spoke to her at the station.

p.text: The doctor who treated me was very _____.
p.correction: The doctor who treated me was very professional.
p.explanation: After 'was very' we need an adjective, so 'professional'.

p.text: Everyone who came to the party agreed it was an _____ evening.
p.correction: Everyone who came to the party agreed it was an enjoyable evening.
p.explanation: Between 'an' and 'evening' we need an adjective: 'enjoyable'.

p.text: She has two brothers, both of who are doctors.
p.correction: She has two brothers, both of whom are doctors.
p.explanation: After a preposition such as 'of' we must use 'whom', not 'who'.

p.text: The house, the roof of which was damaged by the storm, is for sale.
p.correction: The house, the roof of which was damaged by the storm, is for sale.
p.explanation: 'The roof of which' is a correct way to say 'whose roof' for a thing.

p.text: The tools with that he repaired the clock were very old.
p.correction: The tools with which he repaired the clock were very old.
p.explanation: We cannot use 'that' straight after a preposition. Use 'which'.

p.text: Students _____ essays are late will lose marks.
p.correction: Students whose essays are late will lose marks.
p.explanation: 'Whose' shows that the essays belong to the students. 'Who's' means 'who is', which does not fit.

p.text: She won a scholarship, _____ allowed her to study abroad.
p.correction: She won a scholarship, which allowed her to study abroad.
p.explanation: 'Which' refers to the whole idea in a comma clause. 'That' and 'what' cannot be used here.

p.text: There were fifty guests, most of _____ I had never met.
p.correction: There were fifty guests, most of whom I had never met.
p.explanation: After 'most of' we use 'whom' for people.

p.text: The man _____ has offered to look after our cat.
p.correction: The man living next door has offered to look after our cat.
p.explanation: A present participle phrase can replace 'who lives' in a defining relative clause.
p.leadInSentence: The man who lives next door has offered to look after our cat.

p.text: The house _____ we used to live has been sold.
p.correction: The house in which we used to live has been sold.
p.explanation: 'Where' can be replaced by 'in which' with the same meaning.
p.leadInSentence: The house where we used to live has been sold.

p.text: The author, whose latest novel was widely praised, is internationally _____.
p.correction: The author, whose latest novel was widely praised, is internationally renowned.
p.explanation: 'Is internationally ...' needs an adjective: 'renowned'.

p.text: What surprised everyone was how quickly she recovered.
p.correction: What surprised everyone was how quickly she recovered.
p.explanation: 'What' here means 'the thing that', so it works as the subject of the sentence.

p.text: The report, the findings of that were published last week, caused outrage.
p.correction: The report, the findings of which were published last week, caused outrage.
p.explanation: After a preposition we must use 'which', not 'that'.

p.text: The committee, several members of which had resigned, was dissolved.
p.correction: The committee, several members of which had resigned, was dissolved.
p.explanation: 'Several members of which' is a correct formal pattern for a group of things.

p.text: The documents, copies of _____ were leaked to the press, are confidential.
p.correction: The documents, copies of which were leaked to the press, are confidential.
p.explanation: After 'of' we need a relative pronoun for things, so 'which'. 'Them' is not a relative pronoun and 'that' cannot follow a preposition.

p.text: The twins, neither of _____ had ever flown, were thrilled.
p.correction: The twins, neither of whom had ever flown, were thrilled.
p.explanation: After 'neither of' we use 'whom' for people.

p.text: He rejected the offer, _____ surprised nobody.
p.correction: He rejected the offer, which surprised nobody.
p.explanation: 'Which' refers back to the whole action and starts a non-defining comma clause.

p.text: We will give you _____.
p.correction: We will give you whatever help you need.
p.explanation: 'Whatever' means 'any ... that', so it replaces 'any' and 'that'.
p.leadInSentence: We will give you any help that you need.

p.text: The architect, whose designs are admired for their _____, won the prize.
p.correction: The architect, whose designs are admired for their originality, won the prize.
p.explanation: After 'their' we need a noun, and 'originality' is the noun form.

p.text: The proposal, which many considered _____, was finally approved.
p.correction: The proposal, which many considered controversial, was finally approved.
p.explanation: 'Considered' is followed by an adjective, so 'controversial'.

p.text: Whomever wants to join the committee should apply in writing.
p.correction: Whoever wants to join the committee should apply in writing.
p.explanation: The word is the subject of 'wants', so we need 'whoever', not 'whomever'.

p.text: The house, in which garden we played as children, has been demolished.
p.correction: The house, in whose garden we played as children, has been demolished.
p.explanation: Showing possession needs 'whose' (or 'the garden of which'), not 'which'.

p.text: It was a question to which nobody had a convincing answer.
p.correction: It was a question to which nobody had a convincing answer.
p.explanation: The preposition 'to' comes before 'which' in this formal pattern.

p.text: What little remained of the village was submerged by the flood.
p.correction: What little remained of the village was submerged by the flood.
p.explanation: 'What little' means 'the little that', a correct nominal relative use.

p.text: _____ you may think of her methods, she gets results.
p.correction: Whatever you may think of her methods, she gets results.
p.explanation: 'Whatever' means 'no matter what'. The others refer to people, time or place.

p.text: She is no longer _____ she was ten years ago.
p.correction: She is no longer what she was ten years ago.
p.explanation: 'What' means 'the person/thing that' and works here. 'Which' and 'that' need a noun before them, and 'whose' shows possession.

p.text: I'll gladly hire _____ presents the strongest portfolio, regardless of age.
p.correction: I'll gladly hire whoever presents the strongest portfolio, regardless of age.
p.explanation: 'Whoever' means 'any person who' and is the subject of 'presents'.

p.text: This is _____ the treaty was signed.
p.correction: This is the very room in which the treaty was signed.
p.explanation: 'In which' combines the preposition and the relative pronoun to describe where the treaty was signed.
p.leadInSentence: The treaty was signed in this very room.

p.text: _____ interviewed.
p.correction: Whoever applies will be interviewed.
p.explanation: 'Whoever' means 'any person who' and forms the subject of the sentence.
p.leadInSentence: No matter who applies, they will be interviewed.
